note: Curated pattern registry for the v10r Pattern MCP. Every path is repo-relative and validated by mcp/validate-registry.ts. Records point to docs and code — they do not duplicate explanations.

patterns.title: Multi-client core (hexagonal domain modules)
patterns.summary: One backend operations layer ($lib/server/[domain]/) serves four clients — human UI, AI tools, REST API, background jobs — via thin wrappers, with zero duplicated business logic.
patterns.when_to_use: Reach for this whenever a backend capability must be reachable from more than one entry point (page action, API route, AI tool, cron job). It is the foundation nearly every other v10r pattern builds on.

docs.note: The full pattern: canonical module shape, client wiring, error contract
Runtime 7-layer view showing where domain modules sit
Where each piece lives; import direction rules

code.note: Per-domain modules; canonical shape is [domain]/queries.ts + mutations.ts (+ service.ts only when orchestration spans multiple infra calls)

invariants: Domain functions must not import from @sveltejs/kit or $app/ — binding to the request cycle breaks tool and job reuse.
AI tools RETURN structured errors — never throw.
The tool manifest is fail-closed: if a tool is not in the manifest, the AI cannot call it; AI tools get a narrower permission set than the human UI.
Tools capture userId by closure — a tool never sees an unauthenticated call.
emulation_notes: Start every new project with this shape even if only one client exists yet — the second client (AI tool or cron) always arrives.
Keep adapters thin: a +page.server.ts action or +server.ts route should validate input, call one domain function, map the result.
patterns.risk: low — structural pattern, no external services

patterns.title: Docs navigation hubs (README-per-directory convention)
patterns.summary: An AI-optimized docs tree where every directory's README.md is a navigation hub with topic tables, so agents read index → target file, never everything.
patterns.when_to_use: Adopt in any repo meant to be read by AI agents: it turns documentation from a pile of files into an addressable index.

docs.note: Root hub — the entry point of the whole convention
Example directory hub with topic tables
Second example hub (AI subsystem)

invariants: Each documentation directory has a README.md acting as a navigation hub: a 2-3 sentence intro plus a topic table showing which file covers what.
Navigation rule: start at docs/README.md and drill down through directory READMEs — read index, then target file, never everything.
emulation_notes: This is a convention, not code — emulate by writing the hubs, not by copying files.
Keep hub intros to 2-3 sentences; the topic table is the payload.

patterns.title: Pattern Index (the README capability map)
patterns.summary: A hand-maintained table in README.md mapping every repo pattern → the doc that explains it, the code that implements it, and the showcase page that proves it (~129 rows, 19 categories).
patterns.when_to_use: Use as the top-level discovery surface for what a reference repo can do; it is the human-readable twin of this MCP's registry.

docs.note: The Pattern Index section itself (anchor #pattern-index)

code.note: Machine source of truth for showcase coverage — index sections mirror it

invariants: Coverage source of truth is src/lib/showcases/registry.ts — a new showcase area there means a new section in the index; a new sublink means a new row.
Drift points to watch: a new docs/blueprint/<area>/ dir, a new src/lib/server/<domain>/ module, or a renamed route.
emulation_notes: Each row must point to docs AND code AND (where possible) a live proof route — a row without proof is a claim, not a pattern.
Keep it hand-maintained but anchored to a machine-readable registry to bound drift.

patterns.title: Component-first UI system (primitives/composites/layout, CVA, tokens)
patterns.summary: A layered component system — Bits UI → primitives (styled atoms) → composites (business logic) → layout (structural wrappers) — styled entirely through CVA → UnoCSS → design-token CSS variables.
patterns.when_to_use: Emulate when a project needs consistent UI at any scale: the layer split keeps styling decisions in one place and bans ad-hoc HTML.

docs.note: Design philosophy hub
Layer system and CVA variant rules
Token architecture (breakpoints, fluid type/space, elevation)
Styling flow and layout primitives

invariants: Never use raw HTML elements when a project component exists — raw <input>/<button>/<select> bypass the design system.
Styling flows through CVA → UnoCSS utilities → token-backed CSS variables; components never hardcode colors or spacing.
Components are zero-margin; layout is gap-based on the spacing scale.
emulation_notes: Adopt the layer vocabulary first (primitive/composite/layout) — it decides where every new component goes.
Port the token file before porting any component; components without tokens re-create the ad-hoc styling problem.

patterns.title: Jobs & scheduling (registry, runner, platform-owned cadence)
patterns.summary: A slug→execute job registry with a unified runner; cadence lives entirely in platform config (Vercel cron vs container setInterval), so switching hosts needs zero job-code change.
patterns.when_to_use: Use for any recurring or background work — the registry/runner split keeps jobs testable and host-portable.

docs.note: The full pattern including cadence ownership

code.note: Registry: slug → execute function, nothing more

invariants: The registry maps a slug to an execute function — nothing more; cadence lives in platform config, the registry has no schedule field.
Every registered job needs a vercel.json cron entry — a slug with no entry never fires.
Cron delivery is at-least-once — jobs must be idempotent.
emulation_notes: Jobs are a client of domain modules (multi-client core): a job body should call the same domain functions the UI calls.
Vercel Hobby tier rejects sub-daily cron schedules at deploy time — plan cadence accordingly.
patterns.risk: medium — touches deploy config and background execution

patterns.title: AI tool manifest & harness split (tool defs, risk metadata, registry)
patterns.summary: Tool definitions are thin wrappers whose risk-tier metadata and per-surface membership live in a registry, with harness concerns (agent loop, compaction, policy) factored out separately.
patterns.when_to_use: Use as soon as an LLM gets tools: the manifest/harness split is what keeps tool permissions auditable and surfaces honest.

docs.note: Tool calling and per-surface tool membership
Harness audit lens: loop, policy, compaction

tests.note: Drift-guards the replay map against the live tool set

invariants: Risk-tiered approval gates, not per-tool needsApproval flags — approval fatigue is reproducible; the tier rule is the working pattern.
executeDeskToolCall is the single door for mutating tool execution (one SSOT).
stepsForScopes caps agent steps per scope (read-only including desk:ask = 3, mutation = 5).
emulation_notes: The manifest is not a single file: meta maps in tools/index.ts + risk vocab in tools/_types.ts + the approval rule in policy/governor.ts together form it.
Write the drift-guard test early — it is what keeps the manifest honest as tools accumulate.
patterns.risk: high — governs what an LLM is allowed to execute

patterns.title: AI surfaces (chatbot vs deskbot split over one guard)
patterns.summary: Two AI surfaces over one shared guard: a read-only, citation-faithful chatbot (Vely) vs an agentic, mutating, approval-gated deskbot — with a showcase-only rag-demo value kept out of production paths.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when one product needs both a safe answer-bot and an acting agent: splitting the surface (not forking the stack) keeps permissions and prompts honest per surface.

docs.note: The surface split and per-surface rules
AI subsystem hub
How the deskbot integrates with the desk

showcases.note: Chatbot showcase; deskbot is live at app route /desk (no showcase)

invariants: The chatbot never emits a DeskEffect and never creates a proposal.
A chatbot tool never carries a desk scope; a deskbot tool always does — topology derives from manifest membership, not a scope artifact.
rag-demo is not a product surface and must not dilute the chatbot.
emulation_notes: Start with the read-only surface; add the mutating surface only with the approval gate (see deskbot-approval-gate).
Route adapters stay thin — both surfaces call the same guard then their orchestrator.
patterns.risk: high — user-facing LLM behavior and permissions

patterns.title: Deskbot approval gate (proposal → approve, plan-gated mutation)
patterns.summary: Write/destructive desk tools never mutate inside the agent loop; they return a requiresApproval sentinel that becomes a proposal (PlanCard), executed only via an approve-route replay that records the real approver and time.
patterns.when_to_use: Mandatory companion to any mutating AI tool: it converts 'the model wants to write' into an auditable human decision.

docs.note: Where the gate sits in the harness
Proposal lifecycle in the desk

invariants: The hard gate is at the tool layer — write/destructive tools return a requiresApproval sentinel; requiresApproval(risk) is the single rule.
Planning is soft guidance, not the gate — shouldRequirePlan only decides whether to instruct the model to plan.
Approval binds execution — the post-approval resume turn is filtered to read-only scopes so it cannot re-mutate.
emulation_notes: An earlier design (inline ConfirmCard with a model-minted confirmed=false→true handshake) was superseded and never shipped — do not emulate it; the proposal→approve flow is the proven shape.
Record who approved and when at the approve route — the audit trail is the point.
patterns.risk: high — the safety boundary for AI mutation

patterns.title: Layered RAG (llmwiki pointer layer over a rawrag kernel)
patterns.summary: A shared rawrag retrieve() kernel (embed → tiers → RRF fusion → drill) feeds two layers: llmwiki TLDR pointer pages as the answer surface over immutable rawrag chunks as the audit trail.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a project needs grounded answers over a corpus: start with read-only search plus citation/provenance before adding any mutating tools.

docs.note: The two-layer architecture
Corpus and ingest door
Graph tier

invariants: The kernel is never forked — a single user_id tenant filter at the chunk level is the corpus boundary; a duplicated filter would be a cross-tenant leak.
Retrieval tools close over userId via buildRetrievalTools({ userId }) — the model cannot forge identity.

Raw chunks are source truth; llmwiki is the compressed pointer layer — the model answers from wiki TLDRs by default and drills into raw chunks only when the user asks for exact wording or challenges a claim.
emulation_notes: 'nRAG' in docs is a concept name only — the code identifier is rawrag/retrieve(); do not search for an nrag module.
Build the raw layer first; the pointer layer compiles from it and can start empty.
patterns.risk: medium — external embedding/LLM providers with quota limits

patterns.title: Retrieval ingest/search endpoints (one ingest door, /api/retrieval/*)
patterns.summary: The RAG corpus is fed and queried through /api/retrieval/* HTTP endpoints plus a unified ingest door: the app runtime and the Bun docs-ingest script share the same pure planChunks() core.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when the corpus must be maintainable from more than one runtime (app UI and scripts) without forking chunking logic.

docs.note: The ingest door pattern
Observability over the pipeline

code.note: Bun script sharing the same planChunks() door

invariants: One ingest door: the standalone script reuses the app's pure planChunks() so both runtimes share one chunking implementation.
Section-parent chunks are stored with embedding = NULL so tier-1 retrieval never surfaces them.
Re-ingest is resume-safe and idempotent.
emulation_notes: Keep the chunker pure (no I/O) — that is what makes the door shareable across runtimes.
Mind embedding-provider daily quotas when re-ingesting a whole corpus.
patterns.risk: medium — writes to the corpus store; provider quotas apply

patterns.title: Agent Experience (AX) surfaces
patterns.summary: Four derived surfaces make the repo consumable by coding agents: a root AGENTS.md contract, raw-markdown doc variants with Accept negotiation, an /llms.txt URL map with in-band prior corrections, and MCP tool errors that carry machine-actionable recovery steps.
patterns.when_to_use: Adopt when a repo's primary consumers are AI agents: it turns passive docs into addressable, self-correcting surfaces without any hand-maintained duplicate content.

docs.note: The full AX layer: surfaces, derivation map, negotiation contract
The hosted MCP surface the Next-actions convention lives on

code.note: Universal agent contract at the repo root
The .md layer + Accept: text/markdown negotiation (303 + Vary + no-store)
/llms.txt built per request from the docs manifest
validate_snippet rule engine (findings are a success; input never echoed)

invariants: Every surface is derived — llms.txt from the docs manifest, .md bodies from the published registry, tool cards from shared JSON; none is hand-maintained.
Every registry-produced MCP error carries a required diag code AND a Next-actions recovery trailer — a new error branch without them is a compile error.
Content negotiation is 303 + Vary: Accept + no-store; each cacheable artifact lives at exactly one URL.
Tool results are text-only and never echo caller input beyond the bounded id reflection.
emulation_notes: Start with AGENTS.md and llms.txt — the standards that won adoption — and advertise them in-page/headers; an unadvertised llms.txt is dead weight.
Make recovery hints structural (a required parameter on the error constructor), not a style guideline reviewers must remember.
patterns.risk: low — read-only derived surfaces; no new state
